overview: The Later Han in this card is the third of north China's Five Dynasties, not the Eastern Han of 25 to 220. Liu Zhiyuan, a Shatuo military governor based at Taiyuan, declared a new regime while Liao forces withdrew after destroying Later Jin. He entered Kaifeng in 947 and adopted Han as the dynastic name. His death in 948 left the young Liu Chengyou facing powerful ministers, regional commanders, fiscal strain, and rebellions. In 950 the emperor's purge killed several leading officials and their families. General Guo Wei survived the order, marched on Kaifeng, and defeated the court army; Liu Chengyou died during the crisis. Guo founded Later Zhou in 951, while Liu Chong maintained a separate Northern Han state from Taiyuan. The atlas stores one coarse polygon dated 947 to 951, covering much of north China but excluding the Sixteen Prefectures. Its outline is identical to the adjacent Later Jin and Later Zhou overlays, a cartographic reuse rather than proof that borders stood still. The card therefore keeps the exact four-year lifetime and treats broader tenth-century evidence as clearly labeled context.

periods.title: 943 to 944: drought and locusts strain Later Jin
periods.summary: Severe drought and locust outbreaks afflicted the Yellow River region before Later Han existed. Harvest loss, hunger, migration, and tax pressure formed part of the world Liu Zhiyuan inherited. This antecedent period supplies environmental context only; it does not extend the dynasty backward to 943.

periods.title: 944 to 945: war intensifies across north China
periods.summary: Later Jin fought Liao while commanders mobilized troops, horses, grain, and transport. Liu Zhiyuan remained military governor at Taiyuan, building influence without yet ruling a Han dynasty. Chronicle detail about shortages and campaigns explains the regime's origins, but the exact target still begins in 947.

periods.title: 945 to 946: provisioning failures weaken Later Jin
periods.summary: Repeated campaigning exposed fragile supply lines, competing commands, and civilian burdens. The Later Jin court distrusted powerful provincial generals as Liao armies advanced. Taiyuan gave Liu Zhiyuan a defensible base, soldiers, and administrative experience, yet no contemporary event in this interval constitutes Later Han's formal foundation.

periods.title: 946 to 947: Liao destroys Later Jin
periods.summary: Liao forces captured Kaifeng and ended Later Jin, then withdrew amid resistance and provisioning problems. Liu Zhiyuan proclaimed himself emperor from Taiyuan and advanced south. The transition was a contested sequence of military decisions, submissions, and withdrawals, not an instantaneous repainting of the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 947 to 948: Liu Zhiyuan establishes Later Han
periods.summary: Liu Zhiyuan entered Kaifeng, adopted the dynastic name Han, and sought to stabilize north China after Liao withdrawal. His Shatuo military background and Taiyuan network helped secure power. He died in 948, leaving a young heir and a court dominated by senior ministers and commanders.

periods.title: 948 to 949: Liu Chengyou rules through senior ministers
periods.summary: The teenager Liu Chengyou succeeded under the reign title Qianyou. Senior ministers handled government while military governors retained dangerous autonomy. The founder's authority could not simply be inherited with the throne, and tensions among palace, bureaucracy, armies, and provincial commands defined the young regime's second year.

periods.title: 949 to 950: rebellions test the young dynasty
periods.summary: Later Han forces suppressed three major regional rebellions, but victory increased the influence of commanders who had saved the throne. War left bodies, damaged communities, and famine victims requiring burial and relief. The court's success therefore solved immediate threats while sharpening fear of its own generals.

periods.title: 950 to 951: purge, revolt, and dynastic replacement
periods.summary: Liu Chengyou ordered leading ministers and their households killed, including the family of Guo Wei. Guo rebelled, defeated the court army, and entered Kaifeng; the emperor died in flight. After a brief succession maneuver, Guo founded Later Zhou in 951 and Later Han ended.

sections.title: Identify the exact dynasty and audit its map

items.text: Exact id later-han-947 denotes the Later Han of the Five Dynasties, founded by Liu Zhiyuan, with Kaifeng as capital and Taiyuan as its original power base. It must remain separate from the Eastern Han, the succeeding Northern Han, Later Jin, and Later Zhou.

The coverage registry records one China overlay and a missing detailed card. No card-index entry, card file, or researched override currently supplies this record. The imported seam metadata already gives 947 to 951, so research refines identity and explanation without stretching a four-year polity into a century.

All fifty historical-basemap snapshots were audited and none contains the exact id. The only feature is one Polygon in the China seams overlay, with one ring, seventeen positions, and bounding box 102 to 122 east by 32 to 40 north.

Kaifeng, Taiyuan, Luoyang, Zhengzhou, Chang'an, Jinan, Xuzhou, Yedu, Hezhong, Songzhou, Fengxiang, Qingzhou, Xiazhou, and Xiangyang test inside. Beijing, Datong, Chengdu, Changsha, Nanjing, Hangzhou, Fuzhou, and Guangzhou test outside. These probes audit geometry, not household allegiance or the exact reach of administration.

The overlay repeats all sixteen boundary segments from Later Jin and again in Later Zhou. That exact reuse is an editorial simplification, especially across a violent succession. Scholarship treats the era as fragmentation with institutional continuity, while the map color provides a locator rather than a border survey.

sections.title: Rule through court, ministers, and provincial commands

items.text: Liu Zhiyuan rose through the military system and declared imperial authority from Taiyuan after Later Jin collapsed. Reaching Kaifeng required commanders, submissions, transport, supplies, and political bargains. A dynastic title established a claim to rule; it did not instantly make every provincial governor obedient.

The founder died after only months in Kaifeng. His young son Liu Chengyou inherited a court where Yang Bin, Shi Hongzhao, Guo Wei, and other senior figures managed affairs. Regency-like ministerial power protected the throne initially, but it also made the emperor fear men controlling soldiers and appointments.

Su Fengji's route into service included composing memorials and official documents for his father before joining Liu Zhiyuan's staff. His biography shows that polished writing, family connections, and administrative usefulness could build a career beside military patronage. Literacy was political work, not merely private refinement.

Empress Li advised using palace stores instead of imposing an immediate levy to reward soldiers in 947. The episode presents an elite woman intervening in fiscal policy and links court treasure to popular burden. It also survives through moralizing history, so one prudent speech cannot describe every decision.

Ouyang Xiu compiled these reign accounts more than a century later and judged rulers through moral history. The modern translation preserves that perspective while supplying notes and institutional context. Court scenes are precious evidence, but reported speeches and character portraits should not be read as stenographic transcripts.

sections.title: Mobilize armies, taxes, transport, and money

items.text: The dynasty depended on professional troops and provincial commands inherited from decades of war. Soldiers expected rewards, while grain, fodder, weapons, clothing, horses, carts, and labor had to reach armies. Fiscal pressure was therefore not abstract accounting; it moved food and materials away from households.

Campaigns against regional rebels in 949 and 950 preserved the throne but empowered commanders who organized victory. The court then treated military capacity as a threat. Later Han's dilemma was structural: it needed strong generals to survive, yet a sufficiently strong general could replace the dynasty.

Han Yuan tongbao bronze cash provides an exact material trace. The British Museum coin is dated 947 to 948, measures 24.5 millimeters, and weighs 3.07 grams. Such catalog data identify an issue and object; they do not reveal wages, prices, or universal access to cash.

The National Museum of China dates Han Yuan tongbao to the Qianyou era, 948 to 950, with recorded diameters of 2.4 to 2.45 centimeters and weights of 3.1 to 3.9 grams. Some reverses carry star or crescent marks, evidence of mint variation rather than secret astronomy.

A Bank of Korea museum example, issued in 948 and about 21 millimeters across, follows the prestigious Tang Kaiyuan tongbao model. Reusing familiar form could make new dynastic currency legible. The square hole helped strings and casting practice; it was not a tiny palace window.

sections.title: See families, women, hierarchy, and social risk

items.text: Empress Li reportedly came from a farming family and married Liu Zhiyuan while he was still a low-ranking soldier. The story connects court memory to rural origins, abduction, and later imperial kinship. Its dramatic biography cannot establish a typical courtship pattern or ordinary women's choices.

The 950 purge targeted households as well as ministers. Guo Wei's relatives were killed when the emperor tried to remove powerful officials, making kinship a channel of both advancement and collective punishment. Elite family security could collapse overnight when political suspicion turned relatives into hostages or enemies.

Five Dynasties epitaphs preserve marriages, parentage, children, offices, moves, deaths, and funeral commemoration, but the surviving sample favors officials and prosperous families. They recover named women and kin strategies more clearly than poor households, servants, displaced people, or children who received no inscribed stone.

Research on the period's epitaph writing finds increased production, especially around high officials and their families. A growing commemorative form does not mean everyone became equally visible. Cost, status, literacy, and burial practice shaped whose household history entered stone and whose grief left no durable text.

Burial locations for northern officeholders cluster around Kaifeng, Luoyang, Taiyuan, and other political centers, revealing mobility and elite networks across changing dynasties. This evidence helps trace families through regime change, but it maps the officeholding class far better than farmers, artisans, soldiers' dependents, or refugees.

sections.title: Work, eat, make things, and inhabit north China

items.text: Most people still secured food through farming, animal care, transport, processing, storage, and exchange, although the short dynasty leaves no household survey. Drought, locusts, armies, and taxation could disrupt each step. Court chronicles notice crisis more readily than the repeated labor that produced ordinary meals.

A tenth-century Hebei Xing-ware jar at the Metropolitan Museum represents northern ceramic skill associated with elite use and long-distance exchange. Its fine body and finish demonstrate specialized production. It cannot prove that a particular Later Han kitchen owned one, or that luxury ware describes common table settings.

A northern Chinese glazed stoneware jar, made in the ninth or tenth century and now in Cleveland, shows durable vessel traditions spanning dynastic labels. Jars served storage or presentation needs, but this object's broad date prevents assigning it to a named Later Han household or a single precise use.

Museum scholarship emphasizes that ceramic production continued during Five Dynasties political division. Kilns, fuel gathering, clay preparation, shaping, glazing, firing, packing, and transport joined many workers. Rapid regime changes could alter patrons and routes without erasing every craft community when a new emperor entered Kaifeng.

Court provisioning and war records mention grain and transport because armies and capitals concentrated demand. Markets, inns, carts, boats, storehouses, and household reserves linked countryside to Kaifeng, but evidence varies sharply by place. A campaign requisition is a crisis snapshot, not a complete shopping list.

sections.title: Learn, write, print, and read a secure sample

items.text: Education had no documented universal school system. Elite boys could learn texts, calligraphy, administration, and composition through families, tutors, local schools, or official connections, while military and craft skills passed through practice. Evidence for girls, poor children, apprentices, and village instruction remains fragmentary rather than absent by definition.

The woodblock Nine Classics project begun in 932 continued across regimes and reached completion in 953. Its editors compared texts and authorized editions, showing institutional continuity around Later Han. The project expanded reproducible canonical texts, but a printed classic was still an object requiring money, access, and literacy.

Ink rubbings transmitted carved writing by pressing damp paper against a surface and applying ink. Museum collections preserve how inscriptions could be copied beyond their monuments. The technique helps scholars study epitaphs today, yet a modern collection does not prove every tenth-century reader personally made rubbings.

A 935 epitaph for Widow Gao survives in standard script and names its calligrapher, Guo Seng. It predates Later Han but securely shows nearby funerary writing practice. Because it belongs to a specific woman and object, it supplies context without being falsely relabeled a dynastic proclamation.

Secure writing sample: 漢元通寶, romanized Hàn yuán tōng bǎo, on Later Han bronze cash of 947 to 950. The script combines a Han character close to regular or cursive forms with three Kaiyuan-style characters. Literal translation: “Han inaugural circulating treasure.” Museums provide the object, attribution, and reading.

sections.title: Watch ritual, art, music, interiors, and leisure

items.text: A bronze mirror with birds and floral motifs, dated to the early or middle tenth century, shows skilled casting and an object used in personal or domestic space. Its decoration can illuminate taste and craft, but the mirror cannot tell historians which dynasty its owner preferred.

Tomb images of musicians from the tenth-century north preserve instruments, performers, and elite ideas of entertainment after death. They support the presence of organized musical performance in the broader period. A funerary ensemble remains commissioned imagery, however, not a recording of every courtyard celebration in Later Han.

Screens shaped elite interiors by dividing rooms, framing bodies, displaying images, and managing privacy. Art history connects these objects with changing tenth-century spatial culture. Their importance helps imagine courtly settings, while evidence for ordinary one-room homes, barracks, workshops, and temporary shelters remains much thinner.

Epitaphs joined family memory, ritual obligation, calligraphy, stonework, and claims about virtue. Their formulas were crafted representations, not neutral biographies. Comparing many inscriptions can reveal marriage and career patterns, but each tomb text also performed respectability for descendants, ancestors, and future readers.

Court chronicles foreground enthronements, mourning, audiences, punishments, omens, and campaigns because those events carried political meaning. Everyday songs, games, storytelling, festivals, and neighborhood sociability rarely receive equal space. Their silence should narrow claims, not turn four busy years into a society without leisure.

sections.title: Treat illness, injury, hunger, and uncertain care

items.text: Medical governance had developed through Sui and Tang institutions, but evidence for a distinct Later Han medical administration is thin. Court physicians, local healers, pharmacies, Buddhist practitioners, households, and midwives may have worked within inherited traditions. The card distinguishes that regional inheritance from a documented four-year national system.

War created wounds, disability, exposure, exhaustion, infection, and bereavement; drought and locusts heightened malnutrition and disease risk. Chronicles record deaths and relief unevenly, usually when disorder affected government. They rarely preserve an ordinary patient's symptoms, caregiver, treatment sequence, cost, recovery, or long-term impairment.

An early Song medical history recalls an opium-poppy drink linked to the earlier Later Tang emperor Mingzong. That tradition demonstrates movement of remedies and court memory around the tenth century, not verified Later Han prescribing. It belongs as comparison only; medicinal poppy cannot be handed to this dynasty by assumption.

After the 950 fighting, the chronicle describes burial of war dead and famine victims and measures to restore order. Such actions addressed public trauma and unburied bodies more directly than a modern hospital would suggest. They reveal emergency response, while named medical personnel and clinical procedures remain undocumented.

Childbirth, infant illness, aging, tooth pain, broken bones, and chronic disease certainly required care, yet reviewed exact-regime sources do not name a midwife, pediatric practice, disability policy, hospital ward, or sanitation officer. Historical honesty keeps those people visible by recording the gap instead of supplying imaginary treatments.

sections.title: Find water, remove waste, and bound sanitation claims

items.text: Kaifeng depended on rivers, canals, wells, carried water, drainage, and flood management across its long history. Archaeology reveals deeply layered cities because repeated rebuilding buried earlier phases. Much excavated infrastructure is Northern Song or later, so it cannot be assigned automatically to the Later Han capital.

The atlas polygon spans the Yellow River, Wei valley, plains, and uplands, environments requiring different water practices. Households, soldiers, animals, farms, workshops, and travelers needed reliable supplies. That necessity does not establish one standardized Later Han aqueduct, well design, water office, or universal access pattern.

Later Kaifeng evidence for streets, bridges, drains, and waterways helps researchers ask where people and goods moved. It does not securely locate a 947 sewer or household toilet. Urban layers can sit vertically close while remaining centuries apart; archaeology requires dating before infrastructure can time travel.

No reviewed source securely documents Later Han toilets, latrines, cesspits, sewers, night-soil collection, refuse rules, street sweeping, bathhouses, or wastewater labor. People necessarily removed bodily and household waste somehow. The evidence does not reveal the facilities, workers, privacy customs, frequency, or health effects.

Armies and dense court neighborhoods concentrated people, animals, fuel, food scraps, manure, ash, and wastewater. Camps and cities therefore posed practical cleaning problems, but the chronicles focus on command and crisis. A silent annalist is not proof of spotless streets, nor proof that nobody cleaned them.

sections.title: Measure achievements, collapse, and human continuity

items.text: Later Han's immediate achievement was restoring a north China court after Liao occupation and Later Jin's fall. Liu Zhiyuan moved from Taiyuan to Kaifeng, secured submissions, and kept inherited institutions working. Four years is brief, yet maintaining taxation, appointments, defense, ritual, and supply still required coordinated labor.

The dynasty issued its own cash while adapting a familiar Kaiyuan design. Han Yuan tongbao joined political naming, calligraphy, bronze production, casting standards, and exchange in one small object. Coinage projects authority efficiently, though finding a coin cannot measure how evenly money circulated among regions or classes.

Suppressing the 949 to 950 rebellions demonstrated administrative and military reach, but the achievement carried a trap. Victorious commanders became more formidable, and the frightened emperor answered with a purge. Later Han shows how success against one danger could magnify another within a decentralized military order.

Guo Wei founded Later Zhou in 951, so the exact polity's successor is Later Zhou and its ending status is dissolution. Liu Chong's Northern Han continued a rival Liu-family claim from Taiyuan, but it was a separate state. People, offices, skills, texts, workshops, and families crossed both transitions.

The card's achievement is precision: it retains 947 to 951, distinguishes namesakes, labels 943 to 947 as antecedent context, and audits every map snapshot. It also refuses to convert a repeated polygon into stable sovereignty. Map colors changed less neatly than rulers, households, and supply lines did.

ending.text: Later Han ended through a court purge and military revolt, not through the disappearance of north China's population. In 950 Liu Chengyou ordered leading ministers and their families killed; Guo Wei escaped the order, rallied his army, defeated imperial forces, and entered Kaifeng. The emperor died during the collapse. After a short attempt to manage succession through another Liu prince, Guo accepted the throne and founded Later Zhou in 951. That makes Later Zhou the direct successor for this exact Kaifeng regime. Liu Chong, the founder's brother, maintained a rival Liu-family state at Taiyuan, conventionally called Northern Han, but it was a separate polity and should not lengthen later-han-947. Officials, soldiers, farmers, craftspeople, religious communities, families, texts, mints, and transport systems continued under new rulers, often with the same practical knowledge and unresolved losses. The atlas reinforces visual continuity by giving Later Jin, Later Han, and Later Zhou an identical coarse outline. The card treats that as cartographic reuse, records dissolution in 951, and keeps the human transition more complicated than the change of dynastic name.
